title: The sermon
hook: Catholics and Orthodox call it a homily; Protestants often a sermon

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Pentecostal service: long praise, open prayer, testimony, the altar call, and a wind you hear but can't hold. Your line was the spirit moves. Where did you feel a breeze? Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

A Sabbath day in Nazareth, his hometown. Jesus goes to the synagogue, as Luke says was his custom, and stands up to read. He's handed the book of the prophet Isaiah, finds a place, and reads about good news to the poor and freedom for captives. Then Luke slows everything down. "And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him." Every eye in the room. Waiting. And he begins with one sentence: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." Today's word is what happens after the reading: homily.

Catholics and Orthodox Christians usually call it a homily. Protestants often call it a sermon. Both name the same moment: the scripture has been read, and now someone stands, or sits, to open it up. First, an old shape. Long before Nazareth, in the book of Nehemiah, the people gather in Jerusalem, by the water gate, to hear the law read aloud, and the text says: "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading." Read it. Give the sense. Help them understand. That's the job. Second, the difference in the words. A homily, in Catholic and Orthodox use, stays close to the readings just heard. It's usually short, and it walks from the page to the table. A sermon, in some Protestant churches, can range more widely, take one passage deep, and run longer. It's often the center of the service, as we saw a few days ago. Same job, different weight. Third, the listener's part. Jesus told a crowd, "Take heed therefore how ye hear." Preaching isn't finished when the preacher sits down. It's finished when somebody carries something out the door. Fourth, the one line. At Nazareth, Luke gives the heart of it in a single sentence. Homilies run longer than that. But what stays, years later, can be one thing a preacher said. A phrase that landed. A story. The rest fades, and that line stays. So a good way to hear any homily, or any sermon, is to listen for the one line to keep.

Here's the practice: summarize a sermon in one line. Settle, and breathe. Bring back a sermon or homily you've heard, recent or long ago. If none comes, use one of these lessons from the past few days instead: the rite, the candle, the oil, the Emmaus road, the boy in the window, the silence, the wind. Turn it over. What was it actually saying? Now squeeze it down to one sentence, short enough to say in a single breath. Say it quietly to yourself, twice. If you pray, you can hand that line to God and ask for help to live it. The bell holds the time.
Homily. What Catholics and Orthodox call the talk that opens up the readings just heard; Protestants often call it a sermon.
Your line: one line to keep. Today, write your one line down somewhere you'll see it tonight, on your hand, a sticky note, the back of a receipt. Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: At Catholic Mass and the Orthodox Divine Liturgy, a priest or deacon gives a homily on the readings just proclaimed; in Protestant services the sermon, often longer, is usually preached by the pastor and frequently stands at the center of worship.

notes: Editor: Luke says 'Sabbath day' and 'he began to say', so 'morning' and 'he says one sentence' were corrected (more words follow in 4:23–27); 'a square' replaced with Nehemiah's water gate; 'many Protestant churches' narrowed to 'some'.
Claims rule: 'Protestants often call it a sermon' follows the index; 'a sermon, in many Protestant churches, can range more widely' keeps one 'many'; soften to 'some' if a Keeper prefers.
Homily vs sermon: the distinction (homily tied closely to the readings, sermon ranging more widely) is a common description, not a strict rule; Anglicans and Lutherans use both words. Confirm.
'Long before Nazareth' (Nehemiah 8) avoids a date. 'In a square in Jerusalem' paraphrases 'the street that was before the water gate' (Nehemiah 8:1); confirm.

Nazareth scene set in a synagogue on the Sabbath, as Luke 4:16 says; told respectfully, without framing the congregation as a foil. Luke 4:22–27 records more words after the first sentence, so the script says Luke gives 'the heart of it' in a single sentence.
Original note gives the lexicon sense of ὁμιλία (association, conversation) ; the link to English homily is not stated under the claims rule. Confirm.

Audit (2026-10-02): quotations checked exact (Luke 4:20–21, Nehemiah 8:8, Luke 8:18). Editor notes that mention 'many Protestant churches' and 'a square in Jerusalem' are stale: the script now says 'some' and 'the water gate'. Orthodox English usage also says 'sermon'; a Keeper may prefer 'Catholics, and often Orthodox Christians, call it a homily'.
